subsection: 5. Africa: Nigeria, the Congo, Tanzania and Angola

notes.h: Background: why Africa's new states began with problems
notes.b: To understand what went wrong and right after independence, you need three starting facts: how the colonial borders were drawn, why the colonial powers let go, and how the Cold War shaped the new states.
points: Colonial rule means control of a territory by an external power, governed for the benefit of the imperial state rather than of the people who lived there.

European powers partitioned Africa in the later nineteenth century, at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85. They drew borders that cut across peoples and joined rival ones together, which is the root of later ethnic tension.

The Second World War weakened the standing of Britain, France, Belgium and Portugal, and African nationalism (the demand for self-government) grew after 1945. Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957 and led the wave.
About seventeen African states became independent in 1960 alone, so independence came to many territories in a very short time.
The Cold War (the rivalry between the USA and the USSR) meant both superpowers competed for influence in the new states. This shaped events in the Congo and Angola in particular.
notes.tip: Examiners reward essays that start from these roots: colonial borders, ethnic policy and the Cold War are the constraints that later explain why independence went so differently in each country.

notes.h: Key concepts: tribalism, the Commonwealth, indirect rule, federation and secession
notes.b: Several terms recur in every case in this subsection. Knowing exactly what each means as historians use it lets you write precise answers.
points: Tribalism was the colonial officials' term for ethnic loyalty (loyalty to your own ethnic group). Colonial policy often defined, fixed and exploited ethnic identities, so the label described something that colonial rule itself had hardened.
The (British) Commonwealth is an association of Britain and its former colonies, and many of them joined on independence, which kept a link with Britain after rule had ended.

Indirect rule meant governing through existing local rulers instead of replacing them. Lord Lugard used it in Nigeria, where the colonial government ruled much of the north through its emirs (Muslim rulers).
A federation is a state in which regions keep their own governments and powers under a central government. Nigeria's regions are the main example.
Secession means a region breaking away from a state to form its own. Katanga seceded from the Congo in 1960 and Biafra from Nigeria in 1967.

The Force Publique was the Belgian Congo's colonial army, and ONUC was the UN operation in the Congo. The Estado Novo was Portugal's authoritarian regime under Salazar, in place from the 1930s until 1974.

The MPLA was one of Angola's three nationalist movements. The Carnation Revolution was the 1974 overthrow of the Portuguese regime in Lisbon, and Zairianisation was Mobutu's 1973 transfer of foreign-owned businesses to Zairian owners.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level short answers ask what a term means (tribalism, secession, Commonwealth) and give one mark for each correct fact, so learn a one-sentence definition of each.

notes.h: Nigeria: colonial amalgamation and the regions, 1914-1954
notes.b: Nigeria began as a British creation that joined very different peoples. How Britain governed it, and how the regions were later organised, set up the rivalries that would break the country in the 1960s.
points: Lord Lugard united the Northern and Southern territories of Nigeria into one colony in 1914. Under indirect rule, the colonial government ruled much of the north through its existing emirs.
Nigeria's three main groups were the Hausa-Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the west and the Igbo in the east. This mattered because each group was concentrated in one part of the country.
The north was predominantly Muslim and the south had large Christian populations, so religion deepened the divide between north and south.
The 1954 federal constitution created three regions, Northern, Western and Eastern, with Lagos as a federal territory.
The regions had their own parliaments and revenue, and the regional parties drew their support on ethnic lines, which made federal politics tense.

The main parties were the Northern People's Congress (NPC), the Action Group (Yoruba west) and the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC, led by Azikiwe, Igbo east), each rooted in one region.
Nigeria's oil came from Oloibiri in the Niger Delta, discovered by Shell-BP in 1956, and exports began in 1958. The oil lay in the Eastern Region, so it later became a source of dispute.
notes.tip: Be ready to explain why Nigeria's federation broke down. The ethnic regional parties and oil in the east are the first links in that chain of causes.

notes.h: Nigeria: independence and the new federation, 1959-1963
notes.b: Independence in 1960 handed power to a federation whose largest party came from the north. The first years showed both how the system was meant to work and where it was already under strain.
points: In the federal elections of December 1959 the NPC won the most seats and formed a coalition with the NCNC, and its leader Abubakar Tafawa Balewa became federal prime minister.

Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a member of the British Commonwealth, with Balewa as prime minister. The Queen remained head of state, represented by a governor-general, Nnamdi Azikiwe from November 1960.
Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963 with Azikiwe as president, so the Queen was no longer head of state. A fourth region, the Mid-West, was also created in 1963.

Regional tension grew in the early 1960s. A political crisis in the Western Region began in 1962, and the elections of 1965 were violently disputed, which weakened trust in the federal system before the army acted.
notes.tip: Keep the people apart: Balewa was prime minister and was killed in January 1966, while Azikiwe was governor-general and then president, and was not killed.

notes.h: Nigeria: coups, massacres and the road to Biafra, 1966-1967
notes.b: In 1966 the army took over, and ethnic violence turned a political crisis into a break-up. The order of events matters, because each step pushed the Igbo-dominated east closer to leaving.
points: 1. On 15 January 1966 army officers led by Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu killed Prime Minister Balewa, the Northern premier Ahmadu Bello and the Western premier Samuel Akintola. The coup was seen as dominated by Igbo officers, which made northerners suspicious of the Igbo.
2. Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi became the first military head of state in January 1966. He was killed in a counter-coup in July 1966, and Lieutenant-Colonel Yakubu Gowon became head of state.
3. Massacres of Igbo people in the north in 1966, in May and again in September-October, killed many thousands. Large numbers fled to the east, which hardened Igbo feeling against the federation.
4. At Aburi in Ghana in January 1967 an attempt to settle the crisis was made, but it failed.
5. On 27 May 1967 Gowon decreed twelve states. This broke up the Eastern Region and cut the Igbo off from most of the oil.

6. Three days later, on 30 May 1967, Lieutenant-Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu (later called Colonel) declared the east the Republic of Biafra. The federal government responded with a blockade of the east.
notes.tip: Gowon's twelve states (27 May 1967) came before Biafra's declaration (30 May 1967) and prompted it, so do not reverse them. Do not mix up Nzeogwu (coup leader), Ironsi (first military head), Gowon (second) and Ojukwu (Biafra).

notes.h: Nigeria: the Biafran War and its end, 1967-1970
notes.b: The Biafran War was a secession and a famine crisis, not simply Nigeria against itself. Biafra had very little international recognition, but the suffering of its people drew worldwide sympathy.
points: The war lasted from July 1967 to 15 January 1970. It caused widespread famine in Biafra, because the blockade cut off supplies.
Estimates of the death toll vary widely, from several hundred thousand to over a million, most of them from starvation and disease. No single figure is reliable.
Only five states recognised Biafra: Tanzania, Gabon, the Ivory Coast, Zambia and Haiti. Recognition was limited to a few states, which left Biafra isolated.
Britain and the Soviet Union supplied arms to the federal government, while France gave covert (secret) support to Biafra.

Many people outside Nigeria were moved by images of starving Biafran children. Joint Church Aid flew relief into Biafra, and Irish missionaries (Holy Ghost Fathers) were prominent, so supplies kept reaching the enclave.

Gowon announced reconciliation, rehabilitation and reconstruction at the end of the war on 15 January 1970. He said there was "no victor, no vanquished", which aimed to bring the Igbo back into the federation.
notes.tip: Examiners reward noting that the Biafran War was a secession and a famine crisis, with recognition limited to a few states. Do not describe Nigeria as the same as Biafra.

notes.b: Belgium ran the Congo as a colony for profit and gave Congolese people almost no training for government. That is why independence in 1960 arrived so suddenly and so badly prepared.
points: King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State from 1885 as his personal possession. Forced rubber collection caused widespread abuses, which Roger Casement and E. D. Morel exposed, and this led to international protest.

The Belgian government took over the colony in 1908. It was ruled by a paternalistic administration (one that treated Congolese like children to be looked after), which gave them little political role.
The colony's wealth lay in minerals including copper, cobalt and diamonds. The Belgian company Union Minière du Haut-Katanga ran the mines of Katanga, mining copper and cobalt.
By 1960 only a handful of Congolese had a university degree. The Force Publique had no Congolese officers, so the new state would have almost no trained administrators or commanders.
Congolese political parties emerged in the late 1950s, including Patrice Lumumba's National Congolese Movement (MNC), which won the most seats in the May 1960 elections.
Riots in Léopoldville in January 1959 shocked Belgian opinion, and King Baudouin soon promised independence but gave no date.
The Round Table at Brussels in January-February 1960 fixed independence for 30 June 1960, only months later, which left almost no time to prepare.
notes.tip: For source questions on the Congo, place the document using the unpreparedness points here and watch for bias: a document may come from one side or from a colonial viewpoint.

notes.h: Congolese independence and the Lumumba crisis, 1960-1961
notes.b: Within weeks of independence the new state had a mutiny, two secessions and a UN intervention. The speed of the collapse is the main evidence for how unprepared it was.
points: On 30 June 1960 Joseph Kasa-Vubu became head of state and Patrice Lumumba became prime minister.
At the independence ceremony King Baudouin praised Belgium's colonial work. Lumumba replied with a speech attacking the humiliations of colonial rule, which offended Belgian opinion.
Soldiers of the Force Publique mutinied on 5-6 July 1960. Attacks on Europeans followed, so Belgium sent troops back to the Congo in July 1960.
Katanga, led by Moïse Tshombe, seceded on 11 July 1960 with Belgian backing, and South Kasai declared its own state in August 1960.
The UN Security Council authorised the UN operation in the Congo (ONUC) in July 1960. It had about 20,000 troops at its height and withdrew in 1964.
Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960 and Lumumba tried to dismiss Kasa-Vubu. Colonel Joseph Mobutu, the army chief of staff, took power on 14 September 1960.
Lumumba, who had appealed to the Soviet Union for help, was confined to his residence under UN guard. He left it in late November 1960 and was captured in December.
Lumumba was flown to Katanga and murdered there on 17 January 1961 with Belgian officers present. Belgium later accepted moral responsibility.
notes.tip: Keep the Congo's leaders apart: Kasa-Vubu was head of state, Lumumba was prime minister, and Mobutu was the army chief who later ruled. Mobutu's coups are 1960 and 1965.

notes.b: Mobutu first took power in 1960 and then seized it for good in 1965. His rule shows how a Cold War ally could keep a weak state together while ruining its economy.
points: Mobutu seized power in a second coup on 24 November 1965, deposing Kasa-Vubu and putting the army in charge of the state.
The country was renamed Zaire in 1971. Mobutu's authenticité campaign banned Christian first names and replaced European suits with the abacost, to stress African identity.
In 1973 Zairianisation transferred foreign-owned plantations and businesses to Zairian owners, mostly Mobutu's associates. The economy collapsed as the copper price fell in 1974-75.
The Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) was the only legal party, so political opposition was suppressed.
The United States, Belgium and France supported Mobutu as a barrier to communism in central Africa. Their help repelled the Shaba invasions of 1977 and 1978 by Katangan exiles from Angola.
Mobutu announced the end of the one-party state in April 1990, under pressure from protests and the end of Cold War support. He stayed in power until he fell in 1997.
notes.tip: For the Cold War strand of an essay on the Congo, remember that Western powers backed Mobutu as a barrier to communism.

notes.h: Tanganyika and Tanzania: peaceful independence under Nyerere, 1961-1964
notes.b: Tanganyika moved to independence without armed conflict under Julius Nyerere and then united with Zanzibar. It is the main example of the opportunities of independence.
points: Tanganyika was German East Africa until 1918, then a British mandate and, from 1946, a UN trust territory. In both cases Britain governed it on behalf of an international body.
Julius Nyerere founded the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU) in 1954 and led it to a majority in the 1960 elections.
Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 with Nyerere as prime minister. It became a republic with Nyerere as president in December 1962.
Zanzibar became independent in December 1963, but a revolution in January 1964 overthrew its Arab-led government. The Afro-Shirazi Party dominated the new regime.
Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on 26 April 1964, and the union was renamed Tanzania in October 1964. Zanzibar kept its own government and its president, Abeid Karume.
In January 1964 the Tanganyika Rifles mutinied against British officers. Nyerere asked Britain for help, Royal Marines put down the mutiny, and the army was then rebuilt.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Tanganyika (the mainland) with Zanzibar (the islands). Tanzania is the 1964 union name. Ordinary Level questions on Nyerere want dated facts in career order.

notes.h: Tanzania: national unity and the break with Britain
notes.b: With no dominant ethnic group, Nyerere built a national identity instead of letting ethnic politics take hold. In foreign policy he was willing to quarrel with Britain over principle.
points: Tanzania was a multi-ethnic state with more than a hundred ethnic groups and no dominant majority, so no single group could claim to speak for the nation.
Nyerere made Swahili the national language and avoided ethnic parties. A shared language and a national identity reduced ethnic conflict after independence.

Nyerere broke off diplomatic relations with Britain in December 1965 over its failure to act against the white minority regime in Southern Rhodesia. The break was over Rhodesia, not over Tanzania's own affairs.
Tanzania nevertheless stayed in the Commonwealth, so it kept the association while criticising British policy.
notes.tip: Use Tanzania's unity as the contrast with Nigeria's Biafran War in an essay on the opportunities and problems of independence.

notes.h: Angola: Portuguese rule and the war of independence, 1961-1974
notes.b: Portugal refused to decolonise, so Angola's nationalists had to fight. The war split them into three movements with different regional and ethnic bases, which later fed a civil war.
points: Portugal under the Estado Novo regime of António de Oliveira Salazar regarded Angola as an overseas province rather than a colony, and it refused to grant independence.

Armed attacks in Luanda on 4 February 1961 began the Angolan war of independence. A rising in the north followed on 15 March 1961, in which many Europeans and Africans were killed and Portuguese reprisals were severe. The war lasted until 1974.
The MPLA, led by Agostinho Neto and founded in 1956, was strongest among the Mbundu and in Luanda.
The FNLA, led by Holden Roberto, was based among the Bakongo in the north.
UNITA, founded in 1966 and led by Jonas Savimbi, was based among the Ovimbundu.
The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 in Lisbon overthrew the Portuguese regime, and the new government agreed to grant independence to Angola.
notes.tip: Do not swap the movements' leaders and bases: MPLA with Neto, FNLA with Roberto, UNITA with Savimbi. Do not confuse the Carnation Revolution (Portugal, 1974) with the start of the war (1961).

notes.b: Independence came in 1975 without agreement between the movements, so the anti-colonial war turned straight into a civil war that the Cold War powers fed.
points: The Alvor Agreement of January 1975 set up a transitional government in which the three movements shared power, but it broke down into fighting.
Angola became independent on 11 November 1975, with the MPLA under Neto holding Luanda.
The civil war between the MPLA and UNITA and the FNLA lasted until 2002. Cuban troops and Soviet aid supported the MPLA, while South African and American support went to its opponents.
Most of the roughly 300,000 Portuguese settlers left Angola in 1975, taking skills and capital with them. This left the new state short of skilled people.
Oil from Cabinda and diamonds became the main sources of revenue.
notes.tip: To answer why Angola's war became a civil war, give the three movements' different ethnic and regional bases together with their different foreign backers.

notes.h: Relations with the former colonial powers
notes.b: Independence did not end the link with the old rulers. Each power kept a different kind of influence, and this is what examiners mean when they ask whether the colonial powers helped or hindered.
points: Britain and Nigeria: Nigeria kept the Queen as head of state until becoming a republic in 1963 and stayed in the Commonwealth. British companies such as Shell-BP dominated the oil industry, and Britain supplied arms to the federal side in the Biafran War.
Belgium and the Congo: Belgium kept large economic interests through the Union Minière and backed Katanga's secession in 1960. Belgium later supported Mobutu.
Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67, before reaching a settlement with it in 1969.
Portugal and Angola: Portugal's refusal to decolonise until 1974 meant Angola faced a long war, and Portugal's exit left Angola with few trained administrators.

Tanzania and Britain: Tanzania remained in the Commonwealth and received British aid, but Nyerere pursued non-alignment (not taking sides in the Cold War) and criticised Western economic influence. He also broke relations over Rhodesia in 1965.
France kept influence in its former colonies through co-operation accords, the franc zone and military agreements. This pattern was later called Françafrique.
notes.tip: In a helped-or-hindered essay, give a verdict at the start and then cover each power's actions: British aid and arms, Belgian interests and intervention, Portuguese late exit and French networks.

notes.h: Tribalism and ethnic politics after independence
notes.b: Ethnic loyalty did not simply survive from the past. Colonial rule shaped it, and after independence politicians in several states built their support on it.
points: Colonial rulers defined and fixed ethnic identities through census categories, languages and indirect rule. Colonial officials then used the term tribalism to describe the ethnic loyalty that this policy had helped to harden.

In Nigeria, each of the three main parties drew its support from one region and one ethnic group. The army's officer corps also divided on regional lines, which contributed to the coups of 1966 and the massacres that followed.

In the Congo, the leading politicians drew support from particular regions and ethnic communities. Lumumba's base was in the east, Kasa-Vubu's party ABAKO drew on the Kongo people in the Léopoldville region in the west, and Tshombe's Conakat drew on the Lunda of Katanga.
Katanga's secession was partly based on the claim that the Katangan people had a separate identity from the rest of the Congo. The national government rejected this claim.

Tanzania's single language, Swahili, and the policy of building a national identity were among the factors that reduced ethnic conflict after independence. This gives a contrast to Nigeria and the Congo.
notes.tip: Colonial borders and ethnic policy are the causes the exam wants for the breakdown of Nigeria's federation and the Congo's chaos. Show that tribalism was partly a colonial creation.

notes.h: Assessment: the problems and opportunities of independence
notes.b: Independence brought real gains and serious dangers, and the balance differed from country to country. The best answers state a judgement and support it with a paired example on each side.
points: Opportunity: independence gave Africans control of their own governments. Nyerere's Tanzania pursued national unity and African development without a civil war.
Problem: the Belgian Congo's rapid independence left the new state with almost no trained administrators or officers, and the army's mutiny and the secession of Katanga followed within weeks.
Opportunity: Nigeria's oil revenue, which grew rapidly after the 1973 oil price rise, gave the federal government resources for reconstruction after the Biafran War.
Problem: the Biafran War and the 1966 coups showed how the federal structure could fail to hold ethnic groups together.
Problem: Angola's long war of independence ended in civil war because the three movements had different ethnic bases and different foreign backers.
Contemporary view: many African leaders saw independence as the end of colonial domination, while the former colonial powers often saw it as the start of a new relationship of trade and aid.
Later view: historians stress that colonial borders, ethnic policies and the Cold War constrained the new states, but they also stress African agency in shaping the outcomes.
Overall judgement: outcomes differed by country, with Tanzania stable, Nigeria and Angola at war and the Congo in crisis, so a balanced answer compares them.
notes.tip: A higher essay on problems of withdrawal needs a developed, dated example for Britain/Nigeria, Belgium/Congo and Portugal/Angola. State your judgement early and keep to it.

keyTerms.definition: The control of a territory by an external power that governed it for the benefit of the imperial state.
The association of Britain and its former colonies, which many African states joined on independence while keeping their own republics.
A term used by colonial officials for loyalty to ethnic groups, which colonial policies often defined, fixed and exploited.
The colonial army of the Belgian Congo, whose Congolese soldiers mutinied against their Belgian officers in July 1960.
The UN operation in the Congo, set up in July 1960 to restore order, prevent foreign intervention and oppose secession.
The coup of 25 April 1974 in Lisbon that overthrew the Portuguese dictatorship and led to the independence of Angola and Mozambique.
The withdrawal of a region from a state to form a separate state, as in Katanga in 1960 and Biafra in 1967.
The British system of governing through existing local rulers and institutions, associated with Lord Lugard in Nigeria.
A state in which power is divided between a central government and regional governments, as in Nigeria's three regions from 1954.
The authoritarian Portuguese regime founded by Salazar, which treated Angola as an overseas province and fought colonial wars until 1974.
The People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola, founded in 1956, led by Agostinho Neto, which held power from independence in 1975.
Mobutu's policy of 1973 that transferred foreign-owned businesses and plantations to Zairian owners.
